title: Using an AED
blurb: Switching on, pad placement, staying safe during analysis and shock, and getting straight back to CPR.
question: CPR is under way on a patient who collapsed in reception, and a colleague arrives with the practice AED. The patient's chest is damp with sweat and there is a medication patch below his right collarbone. What do you do, and what happens straight after the AED delivers a shock?

teach.body: An automated external defibrillator (AED) reads the heart's rhythm through two sticky pads and, if it finds a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia), it tells you to deliver a shock that can reset the heart. It won't shock a rhythm that doesn't need it. RCUK says anyone can use an AED, and all dental clinical areas should have immediate access to one, so it can be used within the first few minutes of a cardiac arrest.

teach.h: Using the AED step by step

steps.label: Switch on
steps.sub: As soon as it arrives; follow the voice prompts

steps.label: Bare chest, attach pads
steps.sub: CPR continues while pads go on

steps.label: Shock advised
steps.sub: Shout 'Stand clear', look, then press shock

steps.label: Resume CPR at once
steps.sub: Shock or no shock: straight back to 30:2

teach.loop: Follow the AED's prompts until help arrives
teach.caption: Fully automatic AEDs shock by themselves after warning you; semi-automatic ones ask you to press the button.

head: Pad
Position
rows: Below the right collarbone, beside the breastbone
Left side, mid-axillary line, below the armpit
teach.caption: The pictures on the pads show the positions. The current then passes through the heart, which sits between them.

teach.h: Never delay CPR for the AED
teach.body: Compressions keep the heart and brain supplied while the AED gets ready. With more than one rescuer, one keeps doing CPR while the other switches the AED on and applies the pads. The only time everyone takes their hands off is when the AED is analysing and when it shocks. Touching the patient during analysis can confuse the reading, and touching during a shock could harm the rescuer.

What to do

Shave the pad area quickly (razor in kit)
Remove it and wipe the skin
Place the pad away from the device
Remove it if it stops correct placement
teach.caption: RCUK's dental equipment list includes a razor and scissors (for clothing) with the AED, plus a spare set of pads.

teach.h: Whatever the AED says, CPR comes next

children.label: Stand clear, shock, then CPR immediately

teach.caption: 'No shock advised' does not mean the patient is fine. If they are still unresponsive and not breathing normally, carry on CPR.

teach.text: After a shock, don't stop to check for a pulse or wait to see if the patient wakes. Restart chest compressions immediately and keep going until the AED tells you to pause again or the patient clearly shows signs of life.

items: Switch the AED on as soon as it arrives; keep CPR going while the pads go on.
Pads: below the right collarbone and on the left side below the armpit.
Dry a wet chest, shave if needed, remove patches, avoid pacemakers.
Hands off during analysis; shout 'Stand clear' and look before the shock.
After a shock, or 'no shock advised', resume CPR immediately.

summary: You can now use an AED safely: switch it on as soon as it arrives without delaying CPR, place the pads correctly, deal with wet skin, patches and pacemakers, keep everyone clear during analysis and shock, and restart CPR immediately whatever the AED advises.

A.q: CPR has started on a collapsed patient and the AED has just arrived. What is the best immediate action?
options: Finish two more minutes of CPR first
Switch it on and attach the pads now
Wait for paramedics to attach the pads
Check for a pulse before using it
A.why: Switch the AED on and apply the pads as soon as it arrives, while a colleague continues CPR.

whyNot.0: Delaying the AED reduces the chance of a successful shock.
whyNot.2: Anyone can use an AED; waiting wastes vital minutes.
whyNot.3: Pulse checks delay defibrillation and aren't needed to use an AED.

A.q: Which is the usual pad placement for an adult?
options: Both pads side by side on the breastbone
One on each shoulder blade at the back
Below the right collarbone and left side
One on the abdomen and one on the neck
A.why: One pad goes below the right collarbone beside the breastbone, the other on the left side in the mid-axillary line below the armpit, so the current crosses the heart.

whyNot.0: Pads side by side wouldn't send the current through the heart.
whyNot.1: Both pads on the back isn't a standard position.
whyNot.3: These positions don't place the heart between the pads.

A.q: The AED announces 'No shock advised'. The patient is still unresponsive and not breathing normally. What should you do?
options: Resume CPR immediately
Stop CPR and wait for help
Move the pads and reanalyse
Recovery position and watch
A.why: If no shock is advised, restart chest compressions straight away and follow the AED's prompts.

whyNot.1: The patient is still in arrest; stopping CPR means no blood flow.
whyNot.2: Moving the pads delays CPR; the AED will reanalyse when it's ready.
whyNot.3: The recovery position is only for a patient who is breathing normally.

B.q: During AED analysis, a team member carries on giving chest compressions. How should this be interpreted?
options: Good practice, as CPR must never pause
Fine, as long as the pads are dry
Wrong, as it can disturb the analysis
Correct for patients with pacemakers
B.why: Nobody should touch the patient during analysis, as movement can interfere with the AED's reading of the heart rhythm.

whyNot.0: Analysis is one of the few moments when CPR must pause briefly.
whyNot.1: Dry pads don't stop compressions interfering with analysis.
whyNot.3: A pacemaker doesn't change the hands-off rule.

B.q: A colleague is about to place a pad directly over a medication patch on the patient's chest. What should be done?
options: Put the pad on top of the patch anyway
Remove the patch and wipe the skin
Skip the AED for this patient
Place both pads on the patient's back
B.why: Remove a medication patch from the pad area and wipe the skin so the pad makes good contact.

whyNot.0: A patch under the pad can reduce contact and cause burns.
whyNot.2: The patch is easily removed; the AED must still be used.
whyNot.3: Moving both pads to the back isn't the fix; just remove the patch.

B.q: In a crowded waiting room, the AED advises a shock. What is the best action?
options: Press shock quickly before anyone moves
Ask bystanders to hold the patient still
Shock only once the room has emptied
Shout 'Stand clear', check, then shock
B.why: Before shocking, shout 'Stand clear' and visually check nobody is touching the patient, then press the shock button.

whyNot.0: Shocking without checking could injure someone touching the patient.
whyNot.1: Nobody should touch the patient during a shock.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the room to empty delays a life-saving shock; checking nobody is touching is enough.

C.q: An adult in cardiac arrest has just been given a shock. What should happen next?
options: Check the pulse for 10 seconds
Restart chest compressions at once
Give two rescue breaths, then wait
Wait for the AED to reanalyse
C.why: After a shock, restart chest compressions immediately and follow the AED's prompts.

whyNot.0: A pulse check delays compressions after the shock.
whyNot.2: CPR restarts with compressions, not breaths followed by waiting.
whyNot.3: The AED reanalyses later; compressions are needed in the meantime.

C.q: A collapsed patient is lying on a wet floor. CPR is in progress and the AED is ready. What is the best action?
options: Use the AED exactly where they lie
Don't use the AED until it is dry
Dry the chest, move from pooled water
Pour water away and shock at once
C.why: Dry the chest so the pads stick, and move the patient away from pooled water before using the AED.

whyNot.0: Pooled water and a wet chest can stop pads sticking and conduct current.
whyNot.1: The AED must still be used; dry and move rather than delay.
whyNot.3: Pouring water around doesn't make it safe; the chest must be dry and the patient clear of water.

C.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a pacemaker bulge below the right collarbone. How should pad placement be managed?
options: Place the pad directly over the bulge
Don't use the AED with a pacemaker
Turn off the pacemaker first
Place the pad away from the device
C.why: Place the pad away from an implanted device; the AED should still be used.

whyNot.0: A pad over the device can reduce the shock reaching the heart.
whyNot.1: A pacemaker is not a reason to withhold defibrillation.
whyNot.2: Dental staff can't switch off a pacemaker, and it isn't needed.

reteach.title: The AED is a coach, not a judge
reteach.question: Think of the AED as a calm coach who talks you through a game. What does the coach need from you?

blocks.body: Once you switch it on, the AED tells you exactly what to do: attach the pads, stand clear, press the button, start CPR. It decides whether a shock is needed, not you. Your jobs are simple: get it on fast, put the pads where the pictures show, keep everyone's hands off when it says so, and get straight back to pushing on the chest the moment it tells you.

blocks.text: The two moments to keep hands off are analysis and shock. At every other moment, someone should be compressing the chest.

explain.body: The AED is switched on and the pads applied the moment it arrives, while CPR carries on. Every minute without defibrillation in a shockable rhythm lowers the chance of survival.

test.q: When should the AED be switched on during a cardiac arrest?
options: As soon as it arrives
After 10 minutes of CPR
When paramedics arrive
Only if breathing stops
test.why: RCUK: switch the AED on as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.

whyNot.1: Waiting reduces the chance of a successful shock.
whyNot.2: The practice team should use it before paramedics arrive.
whyNot.3: It's for any patient who is unresponsive and not breathing normally, and should be used straight away.

explain.body: Right pad below the right collarbone beside the breastbone; left pad on the left side in the mid-axillary line below the armpit. Bare, dry skin; remove patches; keep away from a pacemaker.

test.q: Where does the left (apical) AED pad go on an adult?
options: On the left shoulder
On the left side below the armpit
On the centre of the breastbone
On the upper back
test.why: The apical pad goes on the left side, in the mid-axillary line below the armpit.

whyNot.0: The shoulder is too high and wouldn't place the heart between the pads.
whyNot.2: The centre of the breastbone is where you compress, not where the pad goes.
whyNot.3: The upper back isn't the standard adult position.

explain.body: During analysis nobody touches the patient. Before a shock, shout 'Stand clear', look along the patient to check everyone is clear, then press the button.

test.q: What must you do immediately before pressing the shock button?
options: Give two rescue breaths
Check for a pulse
Check everyone is clear
Remove the AED pads
test.why: Shout 'Stand clear' and visually check that nobody is touching the patient before delivering the shock.

whyNot.0: Breaths would mean someone touching the patient during the shock.
whyNot.1: Pulse checks delay the shock and put hands on the patient.
whyNot.3: The pads must stay on to deliver the shock.

explain.body: After a shock, or if no shock is advised, restart chest compressions immediately. The AED will tell you when to pause again.

test.q: What is the correct action straight after the AED delivers a shock?
options: Wait to see if the patient wakes
Remove the pads and reposition
Put them in recovery position
Resume chest compressions
test.why: Restart chest compressions immediately after the shock and follow the AED's prompts.

whyNot.0: Waiting means no blood flow; compressions must restart.
whyNot.1: Pads stay in place for further analysis.
whyNot.2: The patient is still in arrest until they show signs of life and breathe normally.
